The appropriation for last year was $75,000, bo the additonal expenditure contemplated is in connection with setting up the monument after it arrives.

What the minister has just said would indicate that the government evidently expect the monument will be sufficiently advanced to be placed in position possibly this year. In that connection I should like to say just a word to the minister about the location of the monument seeing that there have been some rumours to the effect that what was originally intended as the site for the national war memorial might be changed. A rumour has been circulated-and I imagine that there is no foundation for it-that some place other than the capital, Ottawa, might be chosen; again with respect to the capital, that the original site proposed, namely Connaught place; might be altered to some other site. I just wish to point out in connection with the monument that the site and all that pertains thereto was very carefully considered before any designs were called for. As the minister will recall, the monument was the result of a competition, almost a world competition; it was open to all artists, sculptors and architects of the British Empire and of the allied and associated powers. The terms and conditions of the competition were all carefully set forth in plans and specifications which were distributed at the time of the competition and which contained a description of the site and photographs of the area and surrounding buildings. I have in my hand a small volume issued by the department of public works in 1925 entitled Conditions of Competition few- National Commemorative War Monument. In the terms and conditions it is set forth that the government desire to have a monument erected in the capital of Canada and that to quote the exact words: "the site of the monument will be on Connaught place in the city of Ottawa, in approximately the position shown on the accompanying plan." Mention is made of the fact that Connaught place was selected as being the most centrally located spot in the city of Ottawa, the idea of the government of the day being that the wish of the people of Canada generally would be that the monument would be placed where it would be seen most readily by visitors to the capital, and most generally by those who are resident in the capital; in other words where its position would permit of its being most generally and favourably viewed. It was agreed at the time that no other site was quite as appropriate as Connaught place. The designs were made in reference to Connaught place, and without a change of the monument in some particulars 74726-55
it will not be possible to locate it elsewhere. As the minister will see, the volume which was sent out by his department in 1925 contained views of Connaught place which were submitted to the sculptors, and all the designs which were sent in had relation to the immediate environment. The government appointed assessors who appraised the various designs and models sent in. The one that seemed the most appropriate was selected, and the monument selected by the assessors has special relations to the particular site named in this volume of conditions.
To show how important it is to retain the selected site I would draw attention to the fact that at the time those who have been awarded this monument pointed out that something would be lost if the site were changed, in that the monument was symbolical of the .response of the new world to the old at the time of war, and that the figures had been arranged so that when the monument was in position the troops would be moving from the west to the east. It is necessary therefore that the monument should be so placed that the movement of the troops passing through the arch, will be from the west to the east and that the Connaught Place site affords in a quite unique way.
I think it is important that that particular site should be kept in mind for the further reason that other large expenditures that have been made by the government were made having in mind the widening of the central area of the city into an open park which would permit of the monument as well as the parliament buildings, being seen from a distance and the farmer as a central feature as parliament hill is approached from the park. As the minister knows we were discussing the other evening the matter of the central park and the question came up then as to what the city had promised to do with respect to the city hall. I am glad to supplement by this further word, what was said the other night, that while there may not have been a specific and legal agreement as to the site of the city hall becoming part of the park, the understanding was that a time would come when both the city hall and the post office building would have to come down, and what was agreed to was that when the time came that either of those buildings was demolished the space thus created would fall into what would be the Confederation park space. If the government of Canada decided to demolish the present post office that space would become part of the open space belonging to the city; similarly if the city decided to demolish the city hall that site would not be built upon again by the city but would become part of the park.

I want to mention, because I may not have occasion to speak of this again, a further reason for keeping in mind the central position in the capital for the location of this monument. The site was selected, as I have said, in relation to the larger plan of central development of the capital. That plan contemplated a time, which may not be very far distant, when the railways which run into the centre of the city will be electrified, and when the railway tracks themselves will be covered over, as they are in approaches to many large cities. If one were to seek to visualize what was in the mind of the government at the time they were planning the expropriations that have already taken place it was that in course of time the station itself would be enlarged to extend farther in the direction of Laurier avenue. Anyone looking at the station to-day will see that it is constructed only in part, that it contemplates an extension to the east corresponding to the portion constructed at present to the west of the central arch. From there on towards the east the railway tracks would be covered and become in the course of time something in the nature of a plaza which would extend along the east bank of the canal and adjoining Nicholas street from where the station is to beyond Laurier avenue as far as what is known as the Deep Out near Echo drive. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is familiar with that portion of the park because up to a certain stage since he has been in office he has himself completed in a very creditable way that park area which lies 'between the canal and Nicholas street all the way from the Union station to the Deep Cut. He himself has been responsible for the direction of that work, and has added since the old buildings thereon were demolished that portion of the open space as park area to what is already park area or driveway on the east side of the canal and which will be an all important part of the larger scheme when completed.
The decision as to the location of the post office can be settled later, when it may be necessary. A suggestion has been made that the government in putting up other departmental buildings might wish to turn the Langevin block into a post office. Again there has been a suggestion that the front portion of the Union station might become the post office, and the station itself be enlarged. This would appear to have everything to commend it. I mention these matters now because they were in the mind of the previous government at the time the general plan was discussed with those who had to do with the setting out of the terms of the competition for the monument, and they may not be known to

members of the present administration or present to the minds of some who are discussing the question at the moment. What I would suggest, if I might be permitted, is that before the monument is put permanently in any place it be erected temporarily in what is regarded as the best site in the capital, and be permitted to stand there until full opportunity has been given to this house to discuss a change of site should that be thought desirable. I believe the monument was erected in Hyde park, in England, temporarily, and there ought to be opportunity of treating it in a similar manner here.
Just one other point. Some suggestion has been made that the monument should be placed on parliament hill. That point too was carefully considered at the time the terms of the competition were arranged. It was pointed out then that already in connection with the parliament buildings there are three memorials which relate to the great war. There is the central column as one comes into the houses of parliament, which carries an inscription commemorative of Canada's participation in the Great war. There is the carillon, symbolical of the service and sacrifice of Canadian men and women in the war, and there is the peace tower. As far as other memorials on parliament hill are concerned I think they have been confined to some association with the political life of the nation as distinct from its other activities.
As to an objection that has been raised by some to a site on or near a thoroughfare, I would point out that in most of the large cities of the world that is precisely where many of the great .memorials are located. In London, England, the Nelson monument is located in Trafalgar square a part of London where the traffic is most dense. Similarly the cenotaph is located in Parliament street near Whitehall, in the centre of the thoroughfare there. The Arc de Triomphe in Paris is in the centre of the Champs Elysees where many thoroughfares converge. I cite these instances in order that this aspect of the matter may be before the government when considering the location of the memorial this year.

I am grateful to my right hon. friend for the clear and comprehensive summary he has given of the plans and ideas which presented themselves to those who suggested this monument. It is true, as he said, that suggestions have been made not in keeping with those he has outlined to-night and, as has already been intimated, a committee of cabinet has been appointed to consider these matters. We are prepared to discuss the whole situation with the city and with those who may be interested in town

planning, and we hope to arrive at the conclusion that will produce the very best results. I can only say that my right hon. friend's suggestions will be brought to the attention of the committee at its first meeting and will be kept prominently before the committee in all conferences and discussions we may have as to these important matters.

I should like to thank the minister for what he has said. May I point out just one further consideration of importance. We are voting this money under the designation "National monument on Connaught place," and whatever has been paid out already has been paid out under appropriations so designated. The designs were for a monument on Connaught place; the moneys have all been appropriated under that heading from 1923 to the present time, and I suggest to the minister that the committee consider whether any alteration of the site at the present time would not involve a breach of the contract both with those who were competitors, and the artists who received the contract. I know that two of the brothers who won the competition came to the capital to view the particular site, and made certain alterations in the original design on the recommendation of the assessors and in order to make the monument, when it was completed, harmonize with the buildings in the immediate environment. I think that is an important consideration to keep in mind.

That is a point I had not noted before. The wording of the vote is exactly the same as it has been in all previous years, and possibly it does irrevocably commit the government to the location of the monument.

I should like to add one further word, because I think all these considerations are important. The portion of the city selected for the monument is known as Connaught place. It will be recalled that the Duke of Connaught, after whom Connaught place is named, was the Governor General of Canada at the commencement of the war. His Royal Highness was resident in Ottawa at that time. This adds a further association Which makes that site if suitable in other respects, particularly appropriate for the location of a national commemorative war monument.

I hope the minister will do that. Perhaps the minister will remember that I drew his attention last year to an important work, when the votes for harbours and rivers were before the committee. On that occasion I drew his attention to the fact that on the Beaver river, one hundred and fifty miles north of North Battleford there are serious rapids, and that these rapids ought to be cleared of the rocks before navigation can be complete from the Beaver river up to the deepwater system of northern Saskatchewan. I drew his attention also to the fact that a sum of $4,000 or $5,000 had been spent by the late government in clearing out these rocks, and the minister said that he would give the matter his consideration. If I remember correctly, after parliament prorogued a letter came from the department saying that the engineer had looked into the situation and had reported that the matter was not very urgent. That is something like taking the matter into consideration. It is a very easy way of getting over it and, of course last year not a dollar was spent. The rocks and rapids are still there and are still an obstacle to the thousands of settlers and tourists, hunters and miners going from the south to the north. May I ask the minister if at 'this time he has anything of a more definite nature to say with regard to doing some constructive work on these rapids in the present year? I am inclined to think the item to which my hon. friend refers is one of those which fell by the wayside in order to arrive at the $14,000,000 reduction promised by the Minister of Finance, and I do not know that conditions have changed. It is possible we may be able to do something this year.

Mr. Chairman, the minister appears to have the idea that there are
no rivers, harbours or lakes of any account in northern Saskatchewan. That gives me an opportunity, perhaps a brief one, to call the attention of the committee to the fact that that is an erroneous conception of the water system of northern Saskatchewan. The time is coming when some money will have to be spent.
For canoes?
If we take you along we will have to have more than a canoe.
I will go along.

The time is coming when more money ought to be spent in clearing the Beaver river rapids of rocks, in order to have a waterway into that northern area. May I say that we now have a first class provincial highway from North Battleford to Meadow Lake, a distance of slightly over one hundred miles. It is one of the best provincial highways in the province. And then from Meadow Lake to Green Lake, another distance of forty-five to fifty miles the highway is not as good. But when we come to Green Lake we come in contact with the river and lake system of northwestern Saskatchewan. As we leave Beaver Lake and follow the Beaver river down to deep water we come in contact with the Beaver river rapids. As I said, there was an expenditure of about $4,000 made in an effort to clear the rapids. Perhaps another $4,000 or $5,000 would completely clear the Beaver river of the rocks I have mentioned. I think that ought to be done. It is not as though a big expenditure was involved, and it will be money well spent. The point I wish to explain is that the playground of western Canada is in northern Alberta, northern Manitoba and northern Saskatchewan. Northwestern Saskatchewan is part of that playground, and when one goes into that new land and sees for himself at first hand he will understand that it is a very favourable part. For instance, from Green Lake to Dore, the point at which deep water begins, is a distance of about fifty miles. There is now a'rough motor road constructed from Green lake to deep water at Dore. That means there is a motor road from North Battleford to Meadow Lake, a distance of over one hundred miles, and from Meadow Lake to Green Lake, and from Green Lake to the foot of the deep water,-practically another one hundred miles. And it is possible now to go by water from North Battle-ford to deep water in a very short time. After getting into deep water one comes into contact with the Beaver river in earnest. It is a magnificent river, in some places as wide as the St. Lawrence, and from fifty-five to seventy-five feet deep. It flows into the river Churchill as do Reindeer Lake, lake Athabaska

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
and Peter Pond Lake all of which of course are connected with lake Churchill, other northern lakes, and Churchill harbour. Into that new land thousands of settlers, miners, tourists and other people are continually coming in the spring, summer and autumn months. The amount of freight going up and down the Beaver river and into lake Churchill and further north and east and west is surprising. As a land for tourists it is indeed hard to surpass.
As this item was before the house I thought it my duty to draw attention to the fine fishing, farming, lumbering and mining potentialities of that great area. If the Beaver river rapids were cleared at the expenditure of a small amount of money the people living in southern Saskatchewan, Alberta, and for that matter Manitoba, who wanted to go north would be able to go north to investigate and get information of that northern area firsthand. They could get to that tourist area cheaper than to many other parts of the dominion. I shall not take up any more of the time of the house but I wanted to bring these facts to the attention of the minister and of the house. I trust the day is not far distant when at the expenditure of a small amount of money these rapids will be cleared. It will be money well spent because it will make more effective a 200 mile motor road, from North Battleford through Meadow Lake and Green Lake to Dore, and thus be instrumental in opening up a lake and river channel three or four hundred miles north of North Battleford extending into the northern hinterland, where there are bound to be great developments in the future.
